newsitem.title: USA: St. Paul Re sees future in securitization.
newsitem.headline: St. Paul Re sees future in securitization.

text.p: St. Paul Re president James Duffy said he believes the time to experiment with new risk securitization products is now, before the next major catastrophe strikes.

St. Paul Re, the reinsurance arm of St. Paul Cos Inc, in December completed one of the industry's first risk securitization deals, a $68.5 million reinsurance transaction that ties investors' returns to the performance of the company's book of business.

The transaction involved the sale of securities, notes and preference shares, to institutional investors, such as pension funds and hedge funds, whose returns will depend on St. Paul Re's underwriting profit.
The more profitable the business, the better the returns.
Duffy, in an interview with Reuters this week, said the company could have obtained additional capital much more easily by buying traditional one-year retrocessional coverage.
But, he said, he believes it was important to take a more farsighted approach.

The next time a catastrophe on the order of a Hurricane Andrew strikes, he said, traditional sources of capital will dry up, leaving insurers and reinsurers without the resources to write new business at just the time when rates will finally be favorable.
"When that marketplace changes, the access to ordinary capital isn't there," Duffy said.
In 1992, just after Hurricane Andrew, it was virtually impossible "to find some retrocessional capacity to allow you to write the business you wrote before," he said.
But catastrophes such as Hurricane Andrew remove so much capacity from the market that rates spike higher and tough market conditions suddenly turn favorable.
"In 1993 and 1994, anyone could have been in our business and made money," Duffy said. "When things are really spiking and taking off, all you need is a pencil."
But risk securitization deals such as St. Paul Re's are still so new that they can't be done very quickly, Duffy said.
He said the transactions take time to structure and then investors need time to learn about them.
By laying the groundwork now, Duffy said he believes the firm is in a much stronger position to do similar deals in the future if needed.
However, he said, St. Paul Re has no near-term plans to do another securitized reinsurance transaction.
The current transaction, executed by Goldman, Sachs and Co's insurance products group, will provide St. Paul Re with additional reinsurance capacity for up to 10 years.
Duffy said he believes such risk securitization transactions will become more common in the future but said he does not believe they will replace traditional reinsurance.
But he also disagreed with those who believe risk securitization has been a failure and has little promise.
Although several other recent attempts at risk securitization have failed, Duffy said he believes St. Paul's transaction worked because St. Paul Re is in the same position as the investors.

Most other proposed risk securitization deals would have directly linked investors' returns to catastrophes. With such catastrophe-linked bonds, returns would be cut by frequent or severe catastrophes.
But in St. Paul's case, "we're in it with them, in the same boat," Duffy said.
